explainer.problem: Given a policy π and a complete model $p(s', r | s, a)$, compute its value function $v_\pi$: the expected return from every state. This is the prediction problem.

derivation.why: The Bellman equation: one step of reward plus the discounted value of where it leads.
Turn the equation into an update; $v_\pi$ is its fixed point (4.5).

example.text: On the 4×4 gridworld from $v_0 = 0$: after one two-array sweep every nonterminal state has $v_1 = -1$; after two, state 1 has $v_2(1) = -1 + \tfrac14(0 - 1 - 1 - 1) = -1.75$ (Figure 4.2 prints −1.7).

advantages: Exact up to the stopping threshold θ; converges to $v_\pi$ whenever $v_\pi$ exists.
The in-place version usually converges faster than the two-array one (p. 91).
limitations: Sweeps the whole state set every iteration, which is expensive for large problems.
With γ = 1 and a policy that can loop for ever it does not converge (Exercise 4.4).

comparisons.point: Value iteration adds a max over actions to the same backup, to find $v_*$ instead of $v_\pi$.
TD(0) estimates the same $v_\pi$ from sampled transitions, without a model.

lines.text: Start with any $V$ and any deterministic $\pi$
Evaluate: sweep with $V(s) \leftarrow \sum_{s',r} p(s',r|s,\pi(s))[r + \gamma V(s')]$ until the largest change is below $\theta$
Improve: for every $s$, remember the old action, then set $\pi(s)$ to an action maximizing $\sum_{s',r} p(s',r|s,a)[r + \gamma V(s')]$
if no state changed its action: stop with $V$ and $\pi$

flags.suggestion: The app keeps the current action whenever it is still among the maximizing actions, so the policy only changes for a strictly better action.

explainer.problem: Find an optimal policy of a finite MDP whose model is known, by alternating complete policy evaluation with greedy policy improvement.

example.text: On the 4×4 gridworld, starting from the equiprobable random policy, $v_\pi$ is −14, −18, −20 or −22. The greedy policy for those values already moves straight to a corner, and evaluating it gives −1, −2, −3: one improvement was enough (p. 98).

advantages: Converges in a finite number of iterations, often very few.
Each policy is at least as good as the last (the policy improvement theorem).
limitations: Every iteration contains a full policy evaluation, itself many sweeps.
As printed, it may never stop if equally good policies alternate (Figure 4.3's caption); the lab keeps an action while it is still best.

comparisons.point: Value iteration cuts each evaluation to a single sweep.
Monte Carlo ES follows the same evaluate-and-improve pattern from sample episodes, without a model.

Return a policy that is greedy with respect to $V$

explainer.problem: Compute the optimal value function $v_*$ (and from it an optimal policy) of a finite MDP with a known model, without running a full policy evaluation between improvements.

derivation.why: Turn it into an update rule: (4.10).

example.text: Gambler's problem with $p_h = 0.4$: value iteration converges to $v_*(50) = 0.4$, $v_*(25) = 0.16$ and $v_*(75) = 0.64$, the values of bold play, and staking all 50 at capital 50 is among the best stakes.

advantages: One simple backup combines evaluation and improvement.
Converges to $v_*$ under the same conditions that guarantee $v_*$ exists.
limitations: Still sweeps every state; impractical for huge state sets (p. 101).
Formally needs infinitely many sweeps; stops when the change Δ is small.

comparisons.point: Policy iteration evaluates each policy fully before improving it.
Q-learning applies the same max backup to sampled transitions, without a model.
